title:
Attention is a neural mechanism for weighting information.
Attention helps a model focus on relevant information.
Attention became central to modern NLP.
Self-attention relates tokens in the same sequence.
Cross-attention relates two different representations or sequences.
Attention can model long-range relationships.
Attention can be combined with RNNs.
Transformers use attention as a central operation.
Attention is commonly described using queries, keys, and values.
A query represents information seeking relevant context.
A key is used for matching with a query.
A value contains information that can be aggregated.
Attention compares queries with keys.
Similarity scores become attention weights.
Attention weights are applied to values.
The weighted values form the attention output.
Dot-product attention is commonly used.
Scaled dot-product attention scales attention scores.
Scaling helps control large dot products.
Self-attention lets a token interact with other tokens.
Bidirectional encoders can attend to both sides of a token.
Autoregressive decoders use causal masking.
Causal masking prevents access to future target tokens.
Multi-head attention uses multiple attention heads.
Each head can learn a different representation subspace.
Different heads can capture different relationships.
Head outputs are concatenated.
A projection combines multi-head outputs.
Transformer encoders use self-attention.
Transformer decoders use masked self-attention.
Encoder-decoder transformers also use cross-attention.
BERT uses transformer encoder attention.
GPT-style models use transformer decoder attention.
Attention supports parallel processing during training.
Full self-attention has quadratic token interaction cost.
Long sequences can require substantial attention memory.
Efficient attention methods target long contexts.
Attention weights are not complete explanations by themselves.
Attention does not guarantee factual correctness.
Attention can help question-answering systems focus on evidence.
Attention can connect question and passage representations.
Attention can help identify relevant passage tokens.
Attention is not itself a complete QA system.
Retrieval, reasoning, and generation can be separate components.
Contextual representations depend on surrounding tokens.
Attention can connect distant tokens directly.

title:
Text classification assigns labels to text.
Text classification converts text into predefined categories.
Input can be a word, sentence, paragraph, document, email, or message.
Output can contain one or more class labels.
Supervised classification uses labeled training examples.
Binary classification has two classes.
Multiclass classification has more than two possible classes.
Multilabel classification allows multiple labels for one input.
Sentiment analysis is a common text-classification task.
Spam detection is a common text-classification task.
Topic classification assigns documents to topics.
Intent classification identifies the purpose of a user message.
Language identification predicts the language of text.
News classification assigns articles to categories.
Question classification identifies question types.
Customer-support systems can classify incoming requests.
Text preprocessing prepares raw text for a model.
Tokenization divides text into tokens.
Tokens may be words, subwords, or characters.
Lowercasing can reduce vocabulary variation.
Stop-word removal can be useful for some classical models.
Stemming reduces words to stems.
Lemmatization maps words to base forms.
Transformer models commonly use subword tokenization.
Bag of Words is a classical text representation.
Bag of Words is also called BoW.
BoW represents text using vocabulary features.
Count-based BoW records term occurrences.
Binary BoW records term presence.
Basic BoW ignores word order.
BoW vectors are often sparse.
TF-IDF means Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency.
TF-IDF weights terms according to document and corpus frequency.
Common terms receive lower IDF weight.
Distinctive terms can receive higher TF-IDF weight.
TF-IDF works well with classical classifiers.
An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of tokens.
A unigram contains one token.
A bigram contains two tokens.
A trigram contains three tokens.
N-grams preserve limited local word order.
Character n-grams can handle spelling variations.
Naive Bayes is a common text-classification baseline.
Multinomial Naive Bayes works with word-count features.
Logistic regression works well with sparse text features.
Support Vector Machines can work well with TF-IDF.
K-nearest neighbors can use vector similarity.
Decision trees can classify numerical text features.
Random forests can classify suitable text features.
CNNs can capture local text patterns.
RNNs can model sequential text information.
LSTMs can model sequence context.
Transformers can create contextual text representations.
BERT can be fine-tuned for text classification.
A classification head produces class scores.
Softmax is common for mutually exclusive classes.
Sigmoid outputs can support multilabel classification.
Cross-entropy is a common classification loss.
Training data is used to learn model parameters.
Validation data can tune hyperparameters.
Test data is used for final evaluation.
Data leakage can produce misleading evaluation results.
Class imbalance occurs when classes have unequal frequencies.
Class weights can increase minority-class importance.
Oversampling can increase minority examples.
Undersampling can reduce majority examples.
Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions.
Precision measures correctness among predicted positives.
Recall measures how many actual positives are detected.
F1-score combines precision and recall.
A confusion matrix shows class prediction errors.
Macro averaging gives equal weight to classes.
Micro averaging aggregates decisions across classes.
Text classification can support question-answering systems.
Question classification can route questions to knowledge-base sections.
Classification can reduce retrieval from unrelated documents.
Classification can be combined with TF-IDF retrieval.
Classification can be combined with embeddings.
Classification alone does not generate a complete answer.
Ambiguous text can be difficult to classify.
Domain changes can reduce model performance.
Rare classes can be difficult to learn.
Poor labels can reduce model quality.
Overfitting reduces generalization to unseen text.
Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple.
Evaluation should use representative test data.

PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
text:
TITLE: Sentiment Analysis
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.

SECTION: Core definitions
Sentiment analysis is the computational identification of opinions, attitudes, or emotional polarity expressed in text.
Opinion mining is a closely related term that focuses on extracting and analyzing opinions from textual data.
Polarity usually represents whether a statement is positive, negative, or neutral.
Binary sentiment classification assigns text to two classes such as positive and negative.
Three-way sentiment classification commonly uses positive, negative, and neutral classes.
Fine-grained sentiment may use labels such as very negative, negative, neutral, positive, and very positive.
Emotion classification differs from sentiment polarity because it can distinguish emotions such as joy, anger, fear, sadness, and surprise.
Subjectivity detection determines whether a text expresses a personal opinion or mainly states objective information.
Sentiment analysis can operate at document, sentence, aspect, or entity level.
Sentiment analysis is commonly treated as a natural language processing task.

SECTION: Levels and granularity
Document-level sentiment assigns one overall sentiment to an entire document.
Sentence-level sentiment assigns sentiment to an individual sentence.
Aspect-based sentiment analysis identifies sentiment toward specific aspects of an entity.
Entity-level sentiment identifies the sentiment associated with a named entity such as a product or organization.
Aspect extraction finds the attributes or features that are being discussed.
Aspect polarity determines whether the opinion about a particular aspect is positive, negative, or neutral.
Opinion target extraction identifies the object or feature toward which an opinion is directed.
Opinion holder extraction identifies the person, group, or source expressing an opinion.
Opinion expression extraction identifies the words or phrases that convey the opinion.
Fine-grained analysis is useful when one sentence contains different opinions about different aspects.

SECTION: Text preprocessing
Tokenization divides text into tokens such as words, subwords, or punctuation symbols.
Normalization can reduce irrelevant variation such as inconsistent capitalization.
Lowercasing can help traditional models but may remove useful information such as emphasis or proper-name distinctions.
Stop-word removal can reduce feature dimensionality but may remove sentiment-bearing words in some tasks.
Negation handling is important because words such as not can reverse or alter sentiment.
Stemming reduces words to approximate roots by removing affixes.
Lemmatization maps inflected words to dictionary base forms.
Emoji processing can preserve useful sentiment signals that would be lost by deleting symbols.
Hashtags may contain sentiment-bearing words and should not automatically be removed.
URLs, usernames, and repeated punctuation may require task-specific normalization.

SECTION: Lexicon-based methods
A sentiment lexicon is a dictionary that associates words or phrases with sentiment values or categories.
Lexicon-based sentiment analysis can work without supervised training data.
Positive and negative word counts are simple lexicon-based sentiment features.
Valence scores can assign numerical strength to sentiment-bearing terms.
Negation can be handled by modifying the contribution of nearby sentiment words.
Intensifiers such as very can increase the strength of a sentiment expression.
Diminishers such as somewhat can reduce sentiment intensity.
Domain-specific lexicons are useful because a word can have different sentiment meanings in different domains.
Lexicon methods may struggle with sarcasm, context, and implicit sentiment.
Combining several lexicons can increase coverage but may also introduce conflicting word scores.

SECTION: Machine learning methods
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier commonly used as a baseline for text classification.
Logistic regression is a strong linear baseline for sentiment classification with sparse text features.
Support vector machines can perform well on high-dimensional text representations.
Decision trees can model nonlinear rules but may be less competitive than linear models for sparse text.
Random forests combine multiple decision trees and can handle nonlinear feature interactions.
Neural networks can learn distributed representations for sentiment classification.
Recurrent neural networks model sequential information and were widely used before transformer models became dominant.
Convolutional neural networks can detect local n-gram-like patterns in text.
Transformers use attention mechanisms to model relationships among tokens.
Pretrained language models can be fine-tuned for sentiment classification using labeled examples.

SECTION: Features and representations
Bag-of-words represents text using counts or binary indicators of vocabulary items.
Term frequency measures how often a term occurs in a document.
TF-IDF reduces the influence of terms that occur in many documents.
Word embeddings represent words as dense numerical vectors.
Contextual embeddings represent a token using its surrounding context.
N-grams capture sequences of adjacent tokens.
Character n-grams can help with spelling variation and noisy user-generated text.
Sentence embeddings represent a complete sentence or passage as a vector.
Feature scaling may be useful for some machine learning algorithms.
Feature selection can reduce noise and computational cost.

SECTION: Context, negation, sarcasm
Negation scope is the portion of text affected by a negating expression.
A sentiment model that ignores negation can incorrectly classify phrases such as not good.
Double negation can produce meanings that differ from simple negative-word counting.
Sarcasm occurs when literal wording differs from the intended attitude or meaning.
Irony can make literal sentiment cues misleading.
Context from previous sentences may be necessary to determine sentiment.
Conversational sentiment may depend on speaker turns and dialogue history.
Domain context can change the sentiment meaning of a word.
Pragmatic cues such as punctuation, emojis, and discourse markers can affect interpretation.
Sarcasm detection is often treated as a separate but related classification task.

SECTION: Evaluation
Accuracy is the proportion of predictions that are correct.
Precision measures the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive.
Recall measures the proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified.
F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
Macro F1 averages class-level F1 scores and gives each class equal weight.
Micro F1 aggregates contributions across classes and is influenced by class frequency.
A confusion matrix shows counts of correct and incorrect predictions by class.
Class imbalance can make accuracy misleading.
Stratified splitting helps preserve class proportions across train and validation sets.
Test data should be kept separate from training and model selection when possible.

SECTION: Applications and limitations
Sentiment analysis is used for analyzing customer reviews.
Businesses can use sentiment analysis to summarize large collections of feedback.
Social media monitoring can use sentiment models to study reactions to products or events.
Support-ticket sentiment can help identify messages that contain dissatisfaction.
Market research can use sentiment analysis as one signal among many qualitative and quantitative measures.
Sentiment analysis can support survey and feedback analysis.
Automated sentiment predictions should not automatically be treated as ground truth.
Bias in training data can cause systematic differences in performance across domains or groups.
Multilingual sentiment analysis requires language-aware resources and evaluation.
Human review can be useful for ambiguous, sarcastic, or high-impact cases.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question asking what sentiment analysis is, retrieve the definition and polarity concepts.
For a question asking about aspect-based sentiment, retrieve aspect extraction and aspect polarity.
For a question about negation, retrieve negation scope and polarity reversal.
For a question about sarcasm, retrieve literal-versus-intended meaning and contextual cues.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve precision, recall, F1, and confusion matrix definitions.
For a question about lexicon methods, retrieve sentiment dictionaries, valence, and their limitations.
For a question about machine learning, retrieve classifiers and text representations.
For a question about preprocessing, retrieve tokenization, normalization, negation, and emoji handling.
For a question about applications, retrieve customer feedback, reviews, and monitoring examples.
For a question about limitations, retrieve domain shift, ambiguity, sarcasm, bias, and human review.

TITLE: Machine Translation
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.

SECTION: Core concepts
Machine translation is the automatic translation of text or speech from one language to another.
The source language is the language of the input.
The target language is the language of the generated translation.
An MT system maps source-language input to target-language output.
Translation quality depends on linguistic structure, context, domain, and training data.
Parallel data contains aligned examples in two languages.
A bilingual corpus can be used to train or evaluate translation systems.
Monolingual data contains text in one language and can support some MT methods.
Language pairs can have very different word order and grammatical structure.
Translation is not simple word substitution because meaning is expressed compositionally.

SECTION: Rule-based and statistical MT
Rule-based machine translation uses linguistic rules, dictionaries, and grammar resources.
Direct translation systems transform source text using relatively shallow mappings.
Transfer-based systems represent source structures and apply language-specific transfer rules.
Interlingua approaches attempt to map different languages into a language-independent representation.
Statistical machine translation learns translation probabilities from bilingual data.
Phrase-based SMT translates sequences of words or phrases rather than isolated words.
Word alignment estimates relationships between source and target tokens.
Translation models estimate how source phrases correspond to target phrases.
Language models help rank fluent target-language sequences in classical SMT.
Decoding searches for a high-scoring target sentence under the model.

SECTION: Neural machine translation
Neural machine translation uses neural networks to generate translations.
Sequence-to-sequence models encode a source sequence and decode a target sequence.
An encoder produces representations of the source input.
A decoder generates target tokens sequentially or using parallel decoding mechanisms.
Attention allows the decoder to focus on relevant source representations.
Transformer architectures use self-attention and became central to modern NMT.
Self-attention allows tokens to interact with other tokens in the same sequence.
Cross-attention connects target-side representations with source-side representations.
Autoregressive decoders generate output tokens conditioned on previously generated tokens.
Some modern translation systems use encoder-decoder transformer architectures.

SECTION: Tokenization and vocabulary
Subword tokenization breaks rare or unknown words into smaller units.
Byte-pair encoding is a common family of subword segmentation methods.
SentencePiece can learn tokenization directly from raw text.
Subword units reduce the number of unknown words compared with word-only vocabularies.
Vocabulary size affects memory, sequence length, and coverage.
Character-level models can represent arbitrary spelling but may require longer sequences.
Language-specific tokenization rules can improve processing for some scripts.
Normalization must account for Unicode and language-specific writing conventions.
Numbers, dates, names, and URLs may need special treatment in translation pipelines.
Tokenization choices can affect both training efficiency and translation quality.

SECTION: Training and inference
Supervised NMT training commonly minimizes a loss between reference and generated target tokens.
Teacher forcing provides reference previous tokens during training in autoregressive models.
Cross-entropy is commonly used as a token-level training objective.
Batching groups examples to improve hardware utilization.
Padding allows variable-length sequences to be processed in batches.
Attention masks prevent models from attending to invalid padding or future tokens when required.
Beam search explores multiple candidate translations during autoregressive decoding.
Greedy decoding chooses the highest-probability next token at each step.
Sampling can generate diverse outputs but is less common for deterministic translation.
Length penalties can influence the preference for short or long candidate translations.

SECTION: Quality and evaluation
BLEU is an automatic metric based primarily on n-gram overlap with reference translations.
BLEU can be useful for comparing systems under consistent evaluation settings.
BLEU does not fully capture meaning preservation or linguistic adequacy.
chrF evaluates character n-gram similarity and can be useful for morphologically rich languages.
TER measures the amount of editing required to transform a system output toward a reference.
COMET-style learned metrics use neural representations to estimate translation quality.
Human evaluation can assess adequacy, fluency, terminology, and errors.
Adequacy concerns how well the translation preserves source meaning.
Fluency concerns how natural and grammatically appropriate the target output is.
Evaluation should use held-out test data and clearly documented language pairs and domains.

SECTION: Translation challenges
Word sense ambiguity occurs when a source word has multiple possible meanings.
Long-distance dependencies can make translation difficult when relevant words are far apart.
Idioms often require meaning-level translation rather than literal substitution.
Named entities may need transliteration, preservation, or established translations.
Low-resource languages have limited parallel training data.
Domain shift occurs when training data differs substantially from the deployment domain.
Code-switching can combine multiple languages within the same input.
Rare terminology can be difficult when it is absent from training data.
Gender and politeness can require information that is implicit or ambiguous in the source.
Pronoun resolution can require context beyond a single sentence.

SECTION: Multilingual and transfer learning
Multilingual MT trains one model to handle multiple language pairs.
Shared parameters can allow knowledge transfer between related languages.
Zero-shot translation attempts to translate between languages without direct parallel training examples.
Language tags can tell a multilingual model which target language to generate.
Transfer learning can improve low-resource translation by reusing multilingual representations.
Related languages may benefit from shared vocabulary and representations.
Unrelated languages may require different tokenization or language-specific adaptation.
Back-translation creates synthetic parallel data from monolingual target-language text.
Knowledge distillation can transfer behavior from a larger translation model to a smaller model.
Parameter-efficient adaptation can update a smaller portion of model parameters for a language or domain.

SECTION: Safety, bias, and practical use
Machine translation can reproduce biases present in training data.
Sensitive content should be handled according to the privacy and security requirements of the application.
Translation errors can be consequential in legal, medical, or safety-critical settings.
Human review is appropriate when translation accuracy has high consequences.
Terminology constraints can help preserve required product or technical terms.
Glossaries can provide approved translations for recurring domain terminology.
Post-editing is the process of correcting machine-generated translations.
Translation memory systems can reuse previously translated segments.
Quality estimation predicts translation quality without necessarily requiring a reference translation.
Deployment monitoring should track language-specific and domain-specific error patterns.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about machine translation, retrieve source language, target language, and automatic translation.
For a question about NMT, retrieve encoder, decoder, attention, and transformer concepts.
For a question about SMT, retrieve phrase-based models, alignments, translation probabilities, and language models.
For a question about BLEU, retrieve n-gram overlap and its limitations.
For a question about low-resource translation, retrieve transfer learning and back-translation.
For a question about beam search, retrieve candidate exploration during decoding.
For a question about tokenization, retrieve subword units, vocabulary, and sequence length.
For a question about translation challenges, retrieve ambiguity, idioms, terminology, and context.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve automatic metrics and human assessment.
For a question about practical deployment, retrieve glossaries, post-editing, privacy, and monitoring.

TITLE: Question Answering
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
text:
TITLE: Question Answering
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.

SECTION: Core definitions
Question answering is an NLP task that produces an answer to a natural-language question.
A QA system receives a question and may use documents, structured data, or a model's learned knowledge.
Open-domain QA allows questions across many topics.
Closed-domain QA restricts questions to a specific subject or knowledge source.
Extractive QA selects an answer span from a supplied context.
Generative QA produces an answer using a language generation model.
Multiple-choice QA selects one option from a set of candidates.
Yes-no QA returns a binary answer when the task permits it.
Conversational QA uses dialogue history to interpret follow-up questions.
Knowledge-base QA maps questions to structured facts or queries.

SECTION: Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation combines information retrieval with generative language modeling.
A retriever selects documents or passages that may contain evidence for a question.
A generator uses retrieved context to formulate an answer.
RAG can reduce dependence on information stored only in model parameters.
Chunking divides documents into smaller retrieval units.
Embeddings represent text as vectors for semantic similarity search.
Vector search retrieves passages whose embeddings are similar to a query embedding.
Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and semantic retrieval signals.
Reranking reorders retrieved candidates using a more detailed relevance model.
Grounded generation asks the generator to answer using retrieved evidence.

SECTION: Question types
Factoid questions usually ask for a specific entity, value, date, or short fact.
Definition questions ask what a concept means.
Why questions ask for causes, reasons, or explanations.
How questions ask for procedures, mechanisms, or methods.
Comparison questions ask about similarities and differences between concepts.
List questions ask for multiple items that satisfy a condition.
Multi-hop questions require combining information from multiple pieces of evidence.
Analytical questions require reasoning over retrieved facts rather than copying one sentence.
Temporal questions depend on dates or time ranges.
Conversational questions may contain references such as it, they, or that concept.

SECTION: Knowledge-base preparation
Knowledge-center documents should use clear topic headings.
Atomic statements are easier to retrieve than long paragraphs containing many unrelated facts.
Consistent terminology improves retrieval and generation.
Definitions should state the concept before adding detailed explanation.
Examples should be labeled so a generator can distinguish them from general rules.
Limitations should be stored alongside methods to reduce overconfident answers.
Synonyms and alternate terminology can improve query matching.
Cross-references can connect related concepts across documents.
Stable identifiers or topic names can help organize a large knowledge base.
Duplicate or contradictory facts should be detected before indexing when possible.

SECTION: Retrieval and chunking
Chunk size affects how much context is available for answering a question.
Very small chunks may omit information needed to interpret a fact.
Very large chunks may reduce retrieval precision because they contain unrelated material.
Overlapping chunks can preserve context across chunk boundaries.
Chunking by headings can preserve semantic structure.
Chunking by sentences creates small atomic retrieval units.
Metadata can include topic, source, section, language, and document identifier.
Metadata filtering can restrict retrieval to the appropriate knowledge domain.
Top-k retrieval returns a specified number of candidate passages.
Reranking can improve the order of candidates before generation.

SECTION: Generation and grounding
A generator should distinguish retrieved evidence from instructions or unrelated text.
Grounded answers should avoid introducing unsupported claims when the evidence is insufficient.
Citation-aware generation can associate answer statements with retrieved sources.
Answer synthesis combines information from multiple retrieved passages.
Context ordering can influence which retrieved evidence the generator uses.
Prompt instructions can require concise answers, definitions, examples, or step-by-step explanations.
Generation temperature can influence output variability.
Lower randomness is often useful for factual QA tasks.
An abstention policy can allow a system to say that the available evidence is insufficient.
Answer length should match the complexity and requested format of the question.

SECTION: Evaluation
Exact match measures whether a predicted answer exactly matches a reference answer under a defined normalization.
Token-level F1 measures overlap between predicted and reference answer tokens.
Retrieval recall measures whether relevant evidence appears among retrieved candidates.
Retrieval precision measures how much of the retrieved set is relevant.
Answer faithfulness measures whether generated claims are supported by available evidence.
Answer relevance measures whether the response addresses the user's question.
Human evaluation can assess correctness, completeness, relevance, and clarity.
End-to-end QA evaluation should separate retrieval errors from generation errors when possible.
Adversarial evaluation tests robustness against misleading or irrelevant context.
Evaluation datasets should match the target domain and language.

SECTION: Failure modes
Hallucination occurs when a generated answer contains unsupported or fabricated information.
Retrieval failure occurs when relevant evidence is not retrieved.
Context contamination occurs when irrelevant or malicious text influences generation.
Ambiguous questions may have multiple valid interpretations.
Outdated knowledge can produce incorrect answers when the knowledge base is not refreshed.
Contradictory documents can cause inconsistent answers.
Entity confusion occurs when the system mixes facts about similarly named entities.
Over-compression can remove important qualifiers from retrieved evidence.
Answer copying can produce awkward or overly long responses.
Failure to abstain can turn uncertainty into an apparently confident incorrect answer.

SECTION: System design and security
Access control should restrict retrieval to documents the user is authorized to access.
Prompt injection can attempt to manipulate a model through retrieved or user-provided text.
Retrieved documents should not automatically be treated as trusted instructions.
Sensitive information should be protected according to the system's privacy requirements.
Logging can support debugging and quality monitoring but should avoid unnecessary sensitive data retention.
Rate limiting can protect QA services from excessive requests.
Caching can reduce repeated retrieval and generation costs.
Latency should be measured across query processing, retrieval, reranking, and generation.
Observability should record enough information to diagnose retrieval and generation failures.
Versioning knowledge sources helps reproduce answers and investigate changes.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about RAG, retrieve retriever, generator, embeddings, chunking, and grounding.
For a question about extractive QA, retrieve answer-span selection from supplied context.
For a question about generative QA, retrieve answer synthesis and grounded generation.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve retrieval metrics, answer metrics, and human evaluation.
For a question about hallucination, retrieve unsupported claims, grounding, and abstention.
For a question about chunking, retrieve chunk size, overlap, headings, and metadata.
For a question about security, retrieve access control, prompt injection, privacy, and logging.
For a question about multi-hop QA, retrieve evidence combination across multiple passages.
For a question about conversational QA, retrieve dialogue history and reference resolution.
For a question about knowledge centers, retrieve atomic statements, headings, synonyms, and versioning.

TITLE: Text Summarization
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
text:
TITLE: Text Summarization
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.

SECTION: Core concepts
Text summarization creates a shorter representation of a source while preserving important information.
Abstractive summarization generates new wording that represents the source content.
Extractive summarization selects sentences or spans from the source.
Single-document summarization summarizes one source document.
Multi-document summarization combines information from multiple documents.
Query-focused summarization emphasizes information relevant to a specified question or topic.
Generic summarization aims to capture the main content without a specific query.
Headline generation produces very short summaries suitable for titles or headlines.
Meeting summarization condenses dialogue, decisions, and action items.
Long-document summarization requires handling more content than a standard model context may support.

SECTION: Summarization pipeline
Preprocessing prepares the source text for summarization.
Segmentation divides a document into sentences or other units.
Content selection identifies information that should be retained.
Content planning determines an ordering or structure for selected information.
Surface realization generates the final natural-language summary.
Length control specifies a target summary size.
Compression removes redundancy while retaining important facts.
Deduplication reduces repeated information in multi-document summaries.
Attribution can identify which source supports a summary claim.
Post-processing can enforce formatting and length constraints.

SECTION: Extractive methods
Extractive summarization can rank sentences by estimated importance.
Sentence frequency features can identify sentences containing salient terms.
TF-IDF can provide lexical importance features for sentence ranking.
Graph-based methods can represent sentences as nodes and similarity as edges.
Centrality measures can identify sentences that represent central document content.
Position features can be useful in some genres such as news articles.
Redundancy penalties can prevent selecting multiple highly similar sentences.
Maximum marginal relevance balances relevance against redundancy.
Supervised extractive models can learn sentence selection from labeled summaries.
Extractive systems preserve source wording but may produce less fluent summaries.

SECTION: Abstractive methods
Abstractive systems generate summary text rather than only copying source sentences.
Sequence-to-sequence models have been used extensively for abstractive summarization.
Attention helps a decoder focus on relevant source representations.
Transformer models are widely used for modern summarization.
Copy mechanisms can allow models to reproduce important source terms.
Pointer-style mechanisms can help preserve names and rare terminology.
Pretrained language models can be adapted to summarization tasks.
Instruction-tuned generators can summarize text according to explicit formatting requirements.
Abstractive models can paraphrase source information.
Abstractive generation creates a risk of factual errors or unsupported details.

SECTION: Quality and evaluation
ROUGE measures overlap between generated and reference summaries using lexical units.
ROUGE-1 evaluates unigram overlap.
ROUGE-2 evaluates bigram overlap.
ROUGE-L uses a longest-common-subsequence-based comparison.
ROUGE is useful for benchmarking but does not fully measure factuality.
BERT-style semantic metrics compare contextual representations between summaries.
Human evaluation can assess relevance, coherence, readability, and factual consistency.
Faithfulness asks whether the summary is supported by the source.
Coverage asks whether important source information is represented.
Conciseness asks whether the summary avoids unnecessary detail.

SECTION: Factuality and hallucination
Summary hallucination occurs when a summary introduces information not supported by the source.
Entity errors can change names, organizations, locations, or other key facts.
Numerical errors can alter quantities, dates, percentages, or measurements.
Negation errors can reverse the meaning of a source statement.
Cross-document synthesis can accidentally merge facts from different sources.
Attribution errors can associate a claim with the wrong source.
Fact verification can compare generated claims against the source.
Sentence-level source alignment can help identify unsupported summary statements.
Retrieval-based generation can improve access to source evidence but does not guarantee factuality.
High-stakes summaries may require human verification.

SECTION: Long and multi-document summarization
Long-document summarization may require hierarchical processing.
Hierarchical summarization can summarize sections before producing a document-level summary.
Sliding-window processing divides long documents into overlapping segments.
Map-reduce summarization summarizes chunks and then combines their summaries.
Multi-document summarization should identify information shared across sources.
Contradictory sources require explicit handling rather than silent merging.
Source timestamps can matter when summarizing evolving events or records.
Redundancy is a major challenge in multi-document summarization.
Clustering can group related documents or passages before summarization.
Query-focused retrieval can reduce the amount of irrelevant material presented to a summarizer.

SECTION: Practical controls
Maximum output length can constrain summary size.
Bullet summaries can improve scanability for structured information.
Paragraph summaries can preserve more narrative flow.
Audience level can determine how much terminology should be explained.
Style instructions can request formal, simple, technical, or executive summaries.
Key-point extraction can provide a compact alternative to prose summarization.
Action-item extraction focuses on tasks, owners, and deadlines.
Decision extraction identifies conclusions reached in meetings or documents.
Risk extraction identifies stated risks, limitations, or uncertainties.
Summary prompts should clearly identify the source material and desired output format.

SECTION: Applications and limitations
Summarization can support research by reducing the reading burden of long documents.
News summarization can provide concise representations of articles.
Meeting summarization can capture decisions and follow-up actions.
Customer feedback summarization can aggregate recurring themes.
Legal and compliance summaries can help organize documents but may require human review.
Educational summarization can create revision notes from source material.
Summaries can omit details that matter for a particular user.
A concise summary is not necessarily a complete summary.
Model-generated summaries may reflect biases or omissions in the source and model.
Summary quality should be evaluated against the intended use case.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about extractive summarization, retrieve sentence selection and ranking.
For a question about abstractive summarization, retrieve generation, paraphrasing, and factuality.

TITLE: Information Extraction
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
text:
TITLE: Information Extraction
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.

SECTION: Core concepts
Information extraction identifies structured information from unstructured or semi-structured text.
Named entity recognition identifies spans that refer to entities such as people, organizations, and locations.
Entity linking connects a textual mention to an entry in a knowledge base when possible.
Relation extraction identifies relationships between entities.
Event extraction identifies events and their participants, attributes, and triggers.
Attribute extraction identifies properties associated with entities.
Keyphrase extraction identifies important phrases representing a document's content.
Temporal information extraction identifies dates, times, durations, and temporal relations.
Coreference resolution determines when different mentions refer to the same entity.
Information extraction can convert text into structured records suitable for downstream systems.

SECTION: Named entity recognition
Named entity recognition is commonly abbreviated as NER.
Typical NER labels include PERSON, ORGANIZATION, LOCATION, DATE, and MONEY.
Entity label sets vary by domain and application.
BIO tagging represents the beginning, inside, and outside of entity spans.
BIOES tagging adds explicit labels for single-token and ending positions.
Span-based NER predicts entity boundaries and labels directly.
Dictionary-based NER uses lists of known names or terms.
Rule-based NER can use patterns such as capitalization or regular expressions.
Neural NER models can learn contextual representations of entity mentions.
Domain-specific NER may recognize concepts such as diseases, chemicals, products, or legal entities.

SECTION: Relation extraction
Relation extraction identifies semantic relationships between entities in text.
A relation can be represented as a subject, predicate, and object.
Binary relations connect two entities.
N-ary relations can involve more than two participants or arguments.
Relation labels depend on the application and ontology.
Dependency parses can provide syntactic evidence for relations.
Transformer models can classify candidate entity pairs using contextual representations.
Relation extraction can be sentence-level or document-level.
Cross-sentence relations require linking information across multiple sentences.
Relation extraction errors can arise from incorrect entity boundaries or ambiguous context.

SECTION: Event extraction
Event extraction identifies event mentions and their semantic arguments.
An event trigger is a word or phrase that signals an event.
Event arguments are entities or values that participate in the event.
Event roles describe how arguments participate in an event.
Temporal arguments can specify when an event occurred.
Location arguments can specify where an event occurred.
Event coreference determines whether event mentions refer to the same event.
Event schemas define the event types and expected roles for a domain.
Event extraction is useful for building timelines and structured reports.
Implicit events can be harder to extract because they may lack an explicit trigger.

SECTION: Coreference and entity linking
Coreference resolution links mentions that refer to the same underlying entity.
Anaphora occurs when an expression refers back to an earlier mention.
Cataphora occurs when a reference points forward to information introduced later.
Pronouns often require discourse context for correct resolution.
Entity linking maps mentions to canonical identifiers.
Candidate generation produces possible entities for a mention.
Entity disambiguation selects the candidate best supported by context.
Knowledge-base descriptions can provide context for entity linking.
Alias and spelling variation can complicate entity linking.
Entity linking can improve consistency across extracted records.

SECTION: Temporal extraction
Temporal expression recognition identifies phrases referring to time.
Dates can be absolute such as a specific calendar date.
Relative expressions such as yesterday depend on a reference time.
Durations describe how long an event or state lasts.
Temporal normalization maps expressions to standardized representations.
Temporal relation extraction identifies before, after, overlap, or related relations.
Document creation time can help interpret relative temporal expressions.
Time zones can matter when extracting timestamps from global data.
Ambiguous dates require locale or contextual information.
Temporal extraction can support event timelines and scheduling applications.

SECTION: Methods and models
Rule-based extraction uses handcrafted patterns and domain knowledge.
Regular expressions are useful for structured patterns such as identifiers and simple dates.
Dictionaries can provide candidate terms for extraction.
Supervised extraction learns from annotated examples.
Sequence labeling models predict labels for tokens or spans.
Span classification models predict candidate spans and their types.
Dependency parsing can provide syntactic features for rule-based extraction.
Transformer encoders provide contextual representations for many extraction tasks.
Large language models can perform extraction through prompting or structured generation.
Hybrid systems combine rules, statistical models, and generative models.

SECTION: Evaluation and errors
Precision measures how many extracted items are correct among the extracted items.
Recall measures how many relevant items were successfully extracted.
F1 combines precision and recall.
Entity-level evaluation can require exact span and type agreement.
Partial-match evaluation gives different treatment to overlapping but non-identical spans.
Relation evaluation should consider entity identity and relation label correctness.
Error analysis can separate boundary, type, linking, and context errors.
Class imbalance can affect extraction metrics.
Annotation disagreement can indicate that an extraction label is ambiguous.
Evaluation should reflect the ontology and error costs of the target application.

SECTION: Applications and limitations
Information extraction can populate knowledge graphs from text.
Business intelligence systems can extract entities and relationships from reports.
Search systems can use extracted entities and metadata to improve retrieval.
Document processing can extract fields from invoices, forms, and reports.
Scientific text mining can extract experimental entities and relationships.
Customer-support systems can extract issue types, products, and requested actions.
Legal text mining can extract parties, dates, obligations, and cited references.
Extraction quality can degrade when the domain differs from training data.
Private or sensitive documents require appropriate access controls.
Human validation can be necessary when extracted records drive consequential decisions.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about NER, retrieve entity spans, labels, BIO tagging, and domain-specific entities.
For a question about relation extraction, retrieve subject-predicate-object structures and relation labels.
For a question about event extraction, retrieve triggers, arguments, roles, and event schemas.
For a question about coreference, retrieve mention linking, pronouns, anaphora, and context.
For a question about entity linking, retrieve candidate generation, disambiguation, and canonical identifiers.
For a question about temporal extraction, retrieve dates, durations, normalization, and temporal relations.
For a question about methods, retrieve rules, dictionaries, supervised models, transformers, and hybrid systems.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve precision, recall, F1, span matching, and relation correctness.
For a question about applications, retrieve knowledge graphs, search, document processing, and text mining.
For a question about limitations, retrieve ambiguity, domain shift, annotation disagreement, and access control.

PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
text:
TITLE: Dependency and Constituency Parsing
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly knowledge for a generative question-answering system.

SECTION: Core concepts
Parsing analyzes the grammatical structure of a sentence.
Constituency parsing represents a sentence as nested phrases or constituents.
Dependency parsing represents words as nodes connected by directed grammatical relations.
A parse tree is a structured representation of syntactic relationships.
The root of a dependency tree is the main syntactic head of the sentence.
A constituent is a contiguous group of words functioning as a grammatical unit.
A phrase can be categorized as a noun phrase, verb phrase, prepositional phrase, or another phrase type.
Dependency relations connect a dependent word to a head word.
Part-of-speech tags provide lexical categories that can support parsing.
Syntactic parsing is useful for information extraction, question answering, and language understanding.

SECTION: Constituency grammar
A context-free grammar represents productions that describe how constituents can be formed.
A nonterminal symbol represents a syntactic category such as NP or VP.
A terminal symbol represents a word or lexical item in a grammar.
A production rule specifies how a nonterminal can expand.
A sentence can be represented using an S node in traditional grammar notation.
NP commonly denotes a noun phrase.
VP commonly denotes a verb phrase.
PP commonly denotes a prepositional phrase.
Constituency trees are hierarchical and explicitly represent phrase nesting.
Grammar-based parsing searches for a tree consistent with grammar rules and the input sentence.

SECTION: Dependency grammar
Dependency parsing represents grammatical structure using head-dependent relations.
Each non-root token normally has one syntactic head in a basic dependency tree.
The root token is connected to the sentence through the root relation.
Common dependency labels include subject, object, modifier, and case-related relations.
Universal Dependencies provides a cross-linguistic framework for dependency annotation.
Dependency trees can represent long-distance relations without requiring phrase nodes.
Head selection is central to dependency parsing.
Dependency labels encode the grammatical function of a dependent relative to its head.
Dependency graphs are useful for extracting predicate-argument structures.
Dependency parses can support relation extraction and semantic interpretation.

SECTION: Parsing algorithms
Top-down parsing begins with the start symbol and expands grammar rules toward terminals.
Bottom-up parsing builds larger structures from observed tokens.
Chart parsing stores partial results to avoid repeated computation.
CYK parsing is a dynamic-programming algorithm for suitable context-free grammars.
Shift-reduce parsing uses a stack and a sequence of transition actions.
Transition-based dependency parsing predicts actions that construct a dependency tree.
Graph-based dependency parsing scores possible tree structures and searches for a high-scoring tree.
Beam search can keep multiple partial parsing hypotheses.
Dynamic programming can reduce repeated computation in parsing.
Parsing algorithms trade off accuracy, speed, grammar flexibility, and implementation complexity.

SECTION: Ambiguity
Syntactic ambiguity occurs when a sentence can have more than one plausible parse.
Attachment ambiguity occurs when a modifier can attach to different parts of a sentence.
Prepositional phrase attachment is a common source of ambiguity.
Coordination ambiguity can arise when it is unclear how conjuncts are grouped.
Lexical ambiguity occurs when a word has multiple possible grammatical or semantic interpretations.
Probabilistic parsers rank competing parses using learned scores or probabilities.
Context can help resolve syntactic ambiguity.
World knowledge may be needed when syntax alone does not determine the intended interpretation.
Parser errors can propagate into downstream information extraction tasks.
Ambiguity should be considered when interpreting a single parse as definitive.

SECTION: Dependency relations
Nominal subject relations connect a predicate to its grammatical subject.
Direct object relations connect a predicate to an object.
Indirect object relations represent certain recipient or beneficiary structures.
Adjectival modifiers connect descriptive adjectives to nouns.
Adverbial modifiers connect many adverbs or modifying phrases to predicates.
Determiners can represent words such as articles modifying nouns.
Case relations can represent prepositions or case markers in dependency frameworks.
Conjunct relations represent coordination between elements.
Compound relations can represent multiword or compound constructions.
Dependency labels are framework-specific and should be interpreted according to the annotation scheme.

SECTION: Constituency structures
Constituency parsing can reveal nested noun phrases.
Verb phrases can contain auxiliaries, verbs, objects, and modifiers.
Prepositional phrases often contain a preposition and a noun phrase.
Adjective phrases can contain an adjective and its modifiers.
Adverb phrases can contain an adverb and modifiers.
Coordination can be represented as a phrase containing multiple coordinated constituents.
Unary productions contain a single child and may be normalized in some treebanks.
Tree depth measures the level of nesting in a constituency tree.
Span boundaries identify the start and end positions of a constituent.
Constituent labels depend on the grammar or treebank used for training and evaluation.

SECTION: Parsing models and representations
Traditional parsers use manually designed grammars or statistical models.
Probabilistic context-free grammars assign probabilities to grammar productions.
Neural parsers use learned representations rather than only handcrafted rules.
Transformer encoders can provide contextual token representations for parsing.
Graph neural methods can model relationships among candidate syntactic structures.
Character or subword representations can help handle unknown words and morphology.
Pretrained language models can be fine-tuned for dependency or constituency parsing.
Multilingual parsers aim to support multiple languages with shared or language-specific parameters.
Domain adaptation can improve parsing for specialized text.
Parser confidence scores can help downstream systems identify uncertain analyses.

SECTION: Evaluation and applications
Dependency parsing is commonly evaluated using unlabeled attachment score.
Unlabeled attachment score measures whether each token has the correct head.
Labeled attachment score additionally requires the dependency relation label to be correct.
Constituency parsing can be evaluated using bracket or span-based precision and recall.
Exact tree match requires the predicted tree to match the reference under the evaluation definition.
Parsing can support question answering by identifying predicates, subjects, and objects.
Parsing can support information extraction by exposing syntactic relations.
Parsing can support semantic role labeling as a source of syntactic features.
Search and text classification systems can use syntactic features when useful.
Parsing errors should be analyzed by sentence type, domain, and language.

SECTION: Limitations and practical use
Natural language syntax contains ambiguity and exceptions that make perfect parsing difficult.
Informal text may contain fragments, spelling errors, emojis, or unconventional punctuation.
Parser performance can differ substantially across languages.
Treebanks encode annotation conventions that influence what a parser learns.
Domain shift can reduce accuracy when deployment text differs from training data.
Long sentences can be computationally and linguistically challenging.
Coordination and attachment structures can produce difficult errors.
Parsing should be treated as an analysis layer rather than unquestionable truth.
Combining parsing with contextual language models can improve robustness in some settings.
For QA systems, parsing is most useful when its output contributes evidence to a broader reasoning pipeline.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about constituency parsing, retrieve hierarchical phrase structure and grammar rules.
For a question about dependency parsing, retrieve heads, dependents, roots, and dependency labels.
For a question about parsing algorithms, retrieve top-down, bottom-up, chart, transition-based, and graph-based methods.
For a question about ambiguity, retrieve attachment, coordination, lexical ambiguity, and probabilistic ranking.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve UAS, LAS, bracket metrics, and exact tree match.
For a question about dependency relations, retrieve subject, object, modifier, case, conjunct, and compound relations.
For a question about grammar, retrieve terminals, nonterminals, productions, and context-free grammar.
For a question about applications, retrieve QA, information extraction, semantic analysis, and search.
For a question about limitations, retrieve ambiguity, domain shift, informal text, and language variation.
For a question about neural parsing, retrieve contextual representations, transformers, and adaptation.

TITLE: Coreference Resolution
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly NLP knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
USAGE: Each statement is written as an atomic knowledge unit so semantic retrieval can return focused evidence.

SECTION: Core concepts
Coreference resolution identifies mentions in text that refer to the same underlying entity or discourse object.
A mention is a textual expression that refers to an entity or event.
A coreference chain groups mentions that refer to the same entity.
An antecedent is a prior expression that a later reference can point to.
Anaphora occurs when a reference depends on a preceding expression.
Cataphora occurs when a reference points to an expression introduced later.
Pronouns such as he, she, it, and they often require coreference resolution.
Nominal expressions can also participate in coreference chains.
Coreference resolution is a discourse-level NLP task.
Coreference information can support question answering, information extraction, summarization, and dialogue systems.

SECTION: Types of referring expressions
Pronouns are short referring expressions whose interpretation often depends on context.
Proper names can refer to entities introduced elsewhere in a document.
Definite noun phrases can refer to previously established entities.
Indefinite noun phrases can introduce new entities but may also refer to known entities in context.
Demonstratives such as this and that can refer to entities, events, or discourse segments.
Zero anaphora occurs when a reference is omitted but understood from context in some languages.
Event coreference determines whether two event mentions refer to the same event.
Entity coreference focuses on references to people, organizations, objects, and other entities.
Document-level coreference may require information from many sentences.
Conversational coreference can require dialogue history and speaker information.

SECTION: Mention detection
Mention detection identifies candidate spans that may refer to entities.
Rule-based mention detection can use noun-phrase and pronoun patterns.
Named entity recognition can provide useful candidate mentions.
Parsing can help identify noun phrases and grammatical structures.
Neural mention detectors can predict spans directly from contextual representations.
False positive mentions increase the search space for coreference resolution.
False negative mention detection can prevent correct coreference links from being created.
Mention boundaries can affect both coreference and downstream extraction.
Nested mentions may occur when one referring expression contains another.
Some systems perform mention detection jointly with coreference prediction.

SECTION: Coreference linking
Pairwise coreference models score whether two mentions refer to the same entity.
Antecedent ranking models score candidate antecedents for each mention.
Cluster-based methods construct groups of mutually coreferent mentions.
Recency can be a useful but imperfect heuristic for antecedent selection.
Grammatical agreement can provide evidence about candidate compatibility.
Number agreement can distinguish singular and plural candidates in many languages.
Gender agreement can provide evidence when grammatical or semantic gender is expressed.
Semantic compatibility can eliminate implausible antecedents.
Discourse salience can influence which entity a referring expression is likely to denote.
Global inference can improve consistency across a document.

SECTION: Algorithms and models
Traditional coreference systems often combine hand-written rules with statistical ranking.
Rule-based systems can encode constraints for pronouns, names, and noun phrases.
Feature-based machine learning models can rank candidate antecedents.
Neural coreference models use contextual embeddings to represent mentions.
Span-based models score candidate mention spans and possible antecedent links.
Transformer encoders can provide contextual representations for document-level coreference.
Clustering algorithms can group pairwise coreference predictions into chains.
End-to-end systems can jointly learn mention detection and coreference decisions.
Long-context models can help process documents with distant references.
Hybrid systems can combine neural predictions with deterministic linguistic constraints.

SECTION: Linguistic cues
Number agreement can indicate whether a pronoun refers to a singular or plural noun phrase.
Person agreement can help distinguish first-, second-, and third-person references.
Gender agreement can be useful where the language marks gender.
Subject prominence can influence antecedent preferences in some languages.
Parallel grammatical structures can provide clues for resolving references.
Semantic role information can help determine which entity is likely to be referenced.
Discourse topic can make one entity more salient than another.
World knowledge can be necessary to resolve references that syntax alone cannot determine.
Bridging references connect related but not necessarily identical entities.
Ambiguous pronouns may remain unresolved when multiple candidates satisfy the available constraints.

SECTION: Evaluation
Mention detection can be evaluated separately from coreference linking.
Coreference evaluation compares predicted clusters with annotated reference clusters.
MUC is an early metric based on links needed to connect mentions into clusters.
B-cubed evaluates mention-level precision and recall within clusters.
CEAF aligns predicted and reference clusters using a similarity function.
LEA evaluates coreference links while considering entity importance.
CoNLL-style coreference scores commonly aggregate several coreference metrics.
Exact cluster matching is stricter than link-based evaluation.
Evaluation can be sensitive to the mention annotation policy.
Human agreement provides a useful reference for the difficulty of the task.

SECTION: Applications and limitations
Question answering can use coreference to interpret pronouns in questions and documents.
Information extraction can merge facts expressed across multiple mentions of an entity.
Summarization can reduce repetition by recognizing repeated references.
Dialogue systems can use coreference to understand phrases such as that one or they.
Search systems can use entity chains to connect related passages.
Knowledge graph construction can benefit from resolving multiple mentions to one entity.
Long documents increase the number of possible antecedents and candidate links.
World knowledge requirements can make some references difficult to resolve automatically.
Errors in mention detection can propagate through the entire coreference pipeline.
Coreference systems should be evaluated on domains that resemble their deployment environment.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about coreference, retrieve mentions, antecedents, chains, and shared entities.
For a question about anaphora, retrieve references to previously introduced expressions.
For a question about cataphora, retrieve forward references and later-mentioned antecedents.
For a question about pronoun resolution, retrieve agreement, salience, syntax, and discourse context.
For a question about algorithms, retrieve pairwise models, ranking, clustering, span models, and transformers.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve MUC, B-cubed, CEAF, LEA, and aggregated evaluation.
For a question about applications, retrieve QA, extraction, summarization, dialogue, and knowledge graphs.
For a question about mention detection, retrieve candidate spans, noun phrases, NER, and false positives.
For a question about limitations, retrieve long-distance references, world knowledge, ambiguity, and error propagation.
For a question about event coreference, retrieve event mentions, event identity, and discourse context.

TITLE: Semantic Analysis
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly NLP knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
USAGE: Each statement is written as an atomic knowledge unit so semantic retrieval can return focused evidence.

SECTION: Core concepts
Semantic analysis determines aspects of meaning expressed by language.
Lexical semantics studies the meanings and relationships of words and lexical units.
Compositional semantics studies how meanings combine to form larger meanings.
Sentence semantics concerns the meaning of complete sentences.
Discourse semantics studies meaning across multiple sentences and discourse structures.
Semantic representation converts meaning into a structured or vector-based form.
Semantic similarity measures how closely two texts or concepts are related in meaning.
Semantic relatedness is broader than similarity and can include associations between concepts.
Semantic interpretation often uses syntax, context, lexical knowledge, and world knowledge.
Semantic analysis supports question answering, search, translation, summarization, and information extraction.

SECTION: Lexical semantics
Synonymy describes words or expressions with similar meanings.
Antonymy describes contrasting meanings.
Hyponymy describes a specific-to-general semantic relationship.
Hypernymy describes a general-to-specific hierarchy from the perspective of the broader concept.
Meronymy describes a part-to-whole relationship.
Polysemy describes multiple related senses of a lexical item.
Homonymy describes identical forms with unrelated meanings.
Collocation describes words that commonly occur together.
Semantic fields group words associated with a related conceptual domain.
Lexical semantic resources can encode these relationships for NLP systems.

SECTION: Compositional semantics
Compositionality states that the meaning of a larger expression depends on its parts and how they are combined.
Predicate-argument structure represents relationships between predicates and their arguments.
Semantic roles describe functions such as agent, patient, instrument, and location.
Quantifiers express concepts such as every, some, and no.
Negation changes the truth conditions or polarity of an expression.
Modality expresses possibility, necessity, obligation, or related meanings.
Scope describes which part of an expression is affected by an operator such as negation or a quantifier.
Semantic parsing maps natural language to a structured meaning representation.
Logical forms can represent relations and conditions explicitly.
Compositional interpretation can require both syntactic structure and lexical meaning.

SECTION: Semantic representations
Knowledge graphs represent entities and relationships as structured graphs.
Predicate logic can represent entities, relations, quantifiers, and conditions.
Frame semantics represents meaning using frames with associated roles.
Semantic role labeling assigns semantic roles to arguments of predicates.
Distributional representations encode meaning using patterns of word usage.
Word embeddings represent lexical items as vectors.
Contextual embeddings represent tokens according to their surrounding text.
Sentence embeddings represent larger spans as vectors suitable for semantic comparison.
Vector similarity can support semantic search and retrieval.
Symbolic and neural semantic representations can be combined in hybrid systems.

SECTION: Semantic similarity and entailment
Semantic similarity asks how close two expressions are in meaning.
Semantic textual similarity compares the meanings of two text segments.
Natural language inference determines whether one statement entails, contradicts, or is neutral with respect to another.
Entailment means that a hypothesis follows from the information expressed by a premise under the task definition.
Contradiction means that the hypothesis conflicts with the premise.
Neutrality means that the premise does not establish either entailment or contradiction.
Similarity can be lexical, syntactic, semantic, or contextual.
Embedding-based similarity uses vector representations to compare texts.
Cross-encoder models can jointly encode two texts for more detailed comparison.
Semantic matching is important for retrieval and duplicate-question detection.

SECTION: Discourse and context
Discourse context can change the interpretation of an individual sentence.
Coreference links references across sentences.
Discourse relations describe connections such as cause, contrast, elaboration, and sequence.
Topic context can help interpret ambiguous terms.
Temporal context helps determine relationships between events.
Speaker information can affect interpretation in dialogue.
Pragmatics studies how context and communicative intentions influence meaning.
Deixis depends on contextual information such as speaker, time, or location.
Implicit meaning may not be explicitly stated in the words themselves.
Context-aware semantic models can combine sentence and document information.

SECTION: Semantic parsing
Semantic parsing converts natural language into a structured semantic representation.
Task-oriented semantic parsing may map questions to database queries.
Abstract meaning representations can encode relations independently of surface wording.
Frame-based parsing identifies a semantic frame and its roles.
Logical-form parsing can support reasoning over structured knowledge.
Sequence-to-sequence models can generate structured semantic representations.
Constrained decoding can ensure that generated semantic forms follow a required syntax.
Semantic parsers can be evaluated by exact match or execution accuracy when outputs are executable.
Ambiguous language can produce multiple plausible semantic parses.
Domain-specific semantic parsers often use an application-specific ontology.

SECTION: Applications and limitations
Semantic search retrieves content based on meaning rather than only exact word overlap.
Question answering uses semantic interpretation to map questions to relevant evidence.
Information extraction uses semantic relations to structure facts from text.
Machine translation requires semantic interpretation to preserve meaning across languages.
Text summarization benefits from semantic representations that distinguish central information.
Chatbots use semantic analysis to identify user intent and relevant entities.
Semantic analysis can fail when context is missing or world knowledge is required.
Distributional representations may capture associations without explicitly representing logical truth.
Neural semantic models can produce plausible but unsupported interpretations.
High-quality semantic systems should combine context, task constraints, and appropriate evaluation.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about semantic analysis, retrieve lexical semantics, compositional semantics, and context.
For a question about semantic roles, retrieve predicate-argument structure and roles such as agent and patient.
For a question about entailment, retrieve entailment, contradiction, and neutral relationships.
For a question about semantic similarity, retrieve embeddings, vector similarity, and contextual representations.
For a question about semantic parsing, retrieve structured meaning representations and logical forms.
For a question about pragmatics, retrieve context, speaker intent, deixis, and implicit meaning.
For a question about lexical relations, retrieve synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, hypernymy, and meronymy.
For a question about applications, retrieve search, QA, extraction, translation, summarization, and chatbots.
For a question about limitations, retrieve ambiguity, missing context, world knowledge, and neural uncertainty.
For a question about knowledge graphs, retrieve entities, relations, and graph-based semantic representation.
