TITLE: Topic Modeling
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly NLP knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
USAGE: Each statement is written as an atomic knowledge unit so semantic retrieval can return focused evidence.

SECTION: Core concepts
Topic modeling identifies recurring latent themes or topics in a collection of documents.
A topic is represented as a pattern of words that tend to occur together.
Topic modeling is generally an unsupervised or weakly supervised text analysis technique.
Documents can be represented as mixtures of multiple topics.
Topic models are useful for discovering structure in large text collections.
Latent topics are inferred from observed word usage rather than always being manually labeled.
Topic modeling differs from document classification because topics are often learned without predefined classes.
A topic model can provide interpretable summaries of document collections.
Topic distributions can be used as features for downstream tasks.
Topic modeling is commonly applied to research papers, news, reviews, and archives.

SECTION: Latent Dirichlet allocation
Latent Dirichlet allocation, or LDA, is a probabilistic topic model.
LDA represents each document as a mixture of topics.
Each topic in LDA is represented as a probability distribution over words.
Each document has a topic proportion distribution.
The generative view of LDA assumes that documents are produced from latent topic mixtures.
Dirichlet distributions are used as priors over topic proportions and word distributions.
Topic-word probabilities indicate how strongly words are associated with a topic.
Document-topic probabilities indicate how strongly a document is associated with each topic.
LDA inference estimates hidden topic assignments from observed words.
The number of topics is commonly selected as a modeling hyperparameter.

SECTION: Other topic models
Non-negative matrix factorization can discover topic-like components from a document-term matrix.
Probabilistic latent semantic analysis models relationships between documents, words, and latent topics.
Hierarchical topic models organize topics into multiple levels.
Dynamic topic models track topic changes over time.
Neural topic models use neural representations to learn latent topic structures.
Embedding-based topic methods can cluster semantically similar documents or words.
BERTopic-style approaches combine document embeddings, clustering, and topic representation.
Correlated topic models allow topic proportions to exhibit correlations.
Author-topic models connect topics with document authors.
Model choice should depend on corpus size, interpretability requirements, and downstream goals.

SECTION: Preprocessing
Document preprocessing can strongly affect discovered topics.
Tokenization converts documents into processing units.
Stop-word removal can reduce common function words but should be used carefully.
Lemmatization can group related word forms under a common base form.
Stemming can reduce word variants using simpler morphological rules.
Very rare words may add noise to topic models.
Extremely common domain-specific words may dominate topics without adding useful distinction.
N-grams can capture meaningful multiword expressions.
Vocabulary filtering can reduce memory and computation.
Preprocessing should preserve terms that are important for the domain's topics.

SECTION: Topic interpretation
Topic-word rankings are commonly used to inspect the meaning of learned topics.
Top words alone may not always provide a complete interpretation of a topic.
Representative documents can help humans interpret topics.
Topic coherence measures attempt to estimate whether top topic words are semantically coherent.
Human labeling is often useful for assigning readable names to discovered topics.
Topic labels are interpretations rather than necessarily direct outputs of the model.
Two topics can be mathematically distinct but semantically similar.
Topic redundancy occurs when multiple topics represent nearly the same theme.
Topic drift can occur when the same vocabulary changes meaning across time or domains.
Interpretation should consider the corpus and the purpose of the analysis.

SECTION: Evaluation
Topic coherence measures are often used to assess the interpretability of topic-word sets.
Perplexity measures how well a probabilistic model predicts held-out word sequences under its assumptions.
Lower perplexity does not necessarily mean that human readers will find topics more coherent.
Topic diversity measures whether different topics contain distinct high-ranked words.
Human evaluation can ask annotators whether topics are interpretable and distinct.
Downstream evaluation can test whether topic representations improve another task.
Stability evaluation checks whether similar datasets or seeds produce similar topics.
Evaluation should consider both statistical fit and practical interpretability.
The selected number of topics can strongly affect model behavior.
Topic models should be evaluated using held-out data when predictive metrics are used.

SECTION: Applications
Topic modeling can organize large document collections by recurring themes.
Researchers can use topics to explore trends across scientific literature.
News analysis can identify recurring subjects and monitor changes over time.
Customer feedback can be grouped into themes such as delivery, quality, and service.
Search interfaces can use topic labels to help users browse document collections.
Topic distributions can support document recommendation.
Topic modeling can support exploratory analysis before building supervised classifiers.
Historical archives can be analyzed for changes in themes over time.
Topic models can help identify clusters of related documents.
Topic modeling is primarily exploratory and should not automatically be treated as definitive classification.

SECTION: Limitations
Topics are not guaranteed to correspond to human-defined concepts.
Bag-of-words models ignore much of word order and syntax.
Polysemous words can appear in multiple topics for different reasons.
Frequent generic terms can make topics difficult to interpret.
Very short documents may not contain enough information for stable topic inference.
Highly similar topics can be redundant.
Topic assignments can be sensitive to preprocessing and model hyperparameters.
Changing corpora can change the learned topic vocabulary.
Topic models may reflect biases and imbalances in the source collection.
Human interpretation remains important when topic labels are used for decisions.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about topic modeling, retrieve latent themes, document-topic mixtures, and topic-word distributions.
For a question about LDA, retrieve documents, topics, word probabilities, Dirichlet priors, and latent assignments.
For a question about topic coherence, retrieve interpretability and top-word semantic consistency.
For a question about preprocessing, retrieve tokenization, stop words, lemmatization, n-grams, and vocabulary filtering.
For a question about topic interpretation, retrieve top words, representative documents, human labels, and redundancy.
For a question about applications, retrieve document organization, trend analysis, recommendation, and exploratory analysis.
For a question about limitations, retrieve ambiguity, short documents, topic instability, and corpus bias.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve coherence, perplexity, diversity, stability, and human evaluation.
For a question about dynamic topics, retrieve time, topic drift, and changes in vocabulary.
For a question about neural topic modeling, retrieve embeddings, clustering, and latent representations.

TITLE: Chatbots and Conversational AI
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly NLP knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
USAGE: Each statement is written as an atomic knowledge unit so semantic retrieval can return focused evidence.

SECTION: Core concepts
A chatbot is a software system designed to interact with users through natural-language conversation.
Conversational AI refers to systems that use language technologies to understand and generate dialogue.
Task-oriented dialogue systems are designed to accomplish specific goals such as booking or information retrieval.
Open-domain conversational systems can discuss a broad range of topics.
Question answering chatbots answer questions using retrieved knowledge or model knowledge.
Dialogue state represents information accumulated during a conversation.
User intent describes the goal or purpose of a user message.
Entities are important values mentioned in a user's request.
Conversation history provides context for interpreting follow-up messages.
Response generation produces the system's next message.

SECTION: Dialogue pipeline
A basic conversational pipeline can include input processing, intent detection, entity extraction, state tracking, retrieval, and response generation.
Speech-based systems may include automatic speech recognition before language understanding.
Text-based systems receive written user messages directly.
Intent classification maps a message to a predefined task category in task-oriented systems.
Slot filling extracts values needed to complete a task.
Dialogue state tracking updates the system's representation of the current conversation.
Policy selection determines the next system action in traditional task-oriented systems.
Response generation converts the selected action into natural language.
Retrieval components can provide factual passages for grounded responses.
Safety and fallback logic should operate alongside the main dialogue pipeline.

SECTION: Dialogue management
Dialogue management controls how a conversational system responds over multiple turns.
Finite-state dialogue systems represent conversations as predefined states and transitions.
Frame-based systems represent user goals using slots and values.
Policy-based systems choose actions according to dialogue state.
Reinforcement learning can be used to optimize dialogue policies under a defined reward.
Large language models can perform dialogue management through generated reasoning or structured tool calls.
State tracking helps preserve constraints such as dates, locations, and requested items.
Context windows determine how much conversation history is available to the model.
Long conversations may require summarizing or selectively storing earlier turns.
Fallback behavior handles cases where the system lacks sufficient information.

SECTION: Retrieval and tools
Retrieval-augmented chatbots search a knowledge base before generating an answer.
Vector retrieval uses embeddings to find semantically similar passages.
Keyword retrieval can find exact terms and identifiers effectively.
Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and semantic signals.
Reranking can improve the relevance ordering of retrieved passages.
Tool use allows a chatbot to interact with external systems such as databases or APIs.
Structured tool outputs can provide precise values for downstream response generation.
Tool permissions should limit actions to those authorized by the application.
Grounded generation uses retrieved evidence to reduce unsupported claims.
Source attribution can help users inspect the evidence behind an answer.

SECTION: Generative conversational AI
Generative dialogue models produce responses token by token or using other learned generation mechanisms.
Transformer architectures are widely used for conversational language generation.
Instruction tuning teaches models to follow natural-language task requirements.
Dialogue models can maintain context by conditioning on conversation history.
System instructions can define behavior, output format, and constraints.
Temperature and sampling settings can affect response variability.
Lower randomness can be useful when deterministic factual responses are preferred.
Generation can be combined with retrieval to provide current or domain-specific information.
Structured generation can constrain outputs to a required schema.
Human feedback and evaluation can be used to improve conversational behavior.

SECTION: Quality and evaluation
Task success measures whether a task-oriented dialogue achieves its intended goal.
Response relevance measures whether a response addresses the user's message.
Response correctness measures whether factual content is accurate.
Groundedness measures whether factual claims are supported by available evidence.
Dialogue coherence measures whether turns fit together logically.
Consistency measures whether the system maintains compatible information across turns.
User satisfaction can be assessed through surveys or interaction signals.
Latency measures how quickly a conversational system responds.
Fallback rate measures how often the system cannot confidently complete a request.
Human evaluation is useful because conversational quality includes aspects that automatic metrics may miss.

SECTION: Safety and reliability
Chatbots can generate incorrect information even when responses sound confident.
High-impact domains may require stronger verification and human oversight.
Prompt injection can attempt to manipulate a chatbot through user or retrieved content.
Privacy controls should restrict access to personal or confidential conversation data.
Authentication should be used before performing actions on protected accounts.
Authorization determines which actions a user or system is permitted to perform.
Sensitive information should not be exposed merely because it appears in model context.
Audit logs can help investigate tool calls and important system actions.
Rate limits can reduce abuse and resource exhaustion.
Fallback and escalation mechanisms can route difficult cases to humans or safer workflows.

SECTION: Applications
Customer support chatbots can answer common product and service questions.
Educational assistants can explain concepts and generate practice questions.
Enterprise assistants can retrieve information from internal knowledge bases.
Scheduling assistants can help users manage appointments and calendar-related tasks.
Shopping assistants can compare products and answer product questions.
Technical support systems can guide users through troubleshooting procedures.
Research assistants can retrieve and synthesize information from documents.
Healthcare conversational systems require careful safety, privacy, and professional oversight.
Banking and financial assistants require strong authentication and transaction controls.
Conversational interfaces can make complex software functions easier to access.

SECTION: Retrieval and QA cues
For a question about chatbots, retrieve conversational AI, dialogue, intent, entities, and response generation.
For a question about dialogue management, retrieve state tracking, policies, slots, and fallback behavior.
For a question about RAG chatbots, retrieve retrieval, embeddings, reranking, grounding, and attribution.
For a question about generative AI, retrieve transformers, instruction tuning, context, and generation.
For a question about evaluation, retrieve task success, correctness, relevance, groundedness, coherence, and latency.
For a question about chatbot safety, retrieve privacy, authentication, authorization, prompt injection, and escalation.
For a question about applications, retrieve support, education, enterprise assistants, scheduling, and research.
For a question about tool use, retrieve APIs, structured outputs, permissions, and auditability.
For a question about conversation history, retrieve context windows, state tracking, and summarization.
For a question about failures, retrieve hallucination, ambiguity, missing knowledge, and fallback mechanisms.

PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly NLP knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
USAGE: Each statement is written as an atomic knowledge unit so semantic retrieval can return focused evidence.
text:
TITLE: Prompt Engineering
PURPOSE: Retrieval-friendly NLP knowledge for a generative question-answering system.
USAGE: Each statement is written as an atomic knowledge unit so semantic retrieval can return focused evidence.

SECTION: Core concepts
Prompt engineering is the design of instructions and input context used to guide a generative AI model toward a desired output.
A prompt can contain instructions, context, examples, constraints, and a user request.
Prompt design aims to make the requested behavior clear, relevant, and reproducible.
An instruction specifies what the model should do.
Context provides information needed to perform the task.
Output constraints specify the desired structure, length, style, or format.
Examples demonstrate the mapping between inputs and desired outputs.
Prompt templates make recurring tasks more consistent.
Prompt engineering is useful for question answering, extraction, summarization, classification, and generation.
Good prompts reduce ambiguity rather than relying on the model to infer unstated requirements.

SECTION: Prompt components
A system-level instruction can define the overall behavior of an assistant.
A user instruction states the task or request that should be handled.
Context can include retrieved documents or structured data.
Examples can demonstrate the expected input-output pattern.
Constraints can specify forbidden or required output properties.
An output schema can require fields such as answer, evidence, and confidence.
Delimiters can clearly separate instructions from source text.
Explicit variable names can make reusable templates easier to understand.
Task-specific terminology should be defined when ambiguity is likely.
Prompts should avoid unnecessary instructions that compete with the primary task.

SECTION: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting asks a model to perform a task without providing task examples.
Few-shot prompting provides a small number of examples before the new input.
One-shot prompting provides a single example.
Few-shot examples can clarify output format and task interpretation.
Examples should be representative of the target task.
Poor examples can teach unwanted patterns or biases.
Example order can sometimes influence model behavior.
Too many examples can consume context and reduce room for the actual task.
Few-shot prompting is especially useful when a task is difficult to describe with instructions alone.
Zero-shot prompting can be preferable when context limits make examples expensive.

SECTION: Structured output
Structured prompting asks the model to produce a predictable schema such as JSON or a table.
Explicit field definitions reduce ambiguity about the required output.
Enumerated labels can constrain classification outputs.
Schema validation can detect malformed generated data.
Structured outputs are useful for information extraction pipelines.
Consistent field names simplify downstream processing.
Optional fields should be explicitly documented.
Type constraints can distinguish numbers, strings, arrays, and booleans.
Output length constraints can prevent excessive generated text.
Post-processing should not silently reinterpret malformed or unsupported model outputs.

SECTION: Retrieval-augmented prompting
Retrieval-augmented prompting provides external context to a generative model before answer generation.
Retrieved passages should be clearly separated from task instructions.
The prompt can tell the model to answer using only the supplied evidence when grounding is required.
Source identifiers can allow generated claims to be associated with retrieved passages.
Context selection affects answer quality because irrelevant evidence can distract the model.
Retrieved context should be relevant, sufficiently complete, and within the model's context capacity.
Conflicting sources should be handled explicitly rather than silently merged.
An abstention instruction can tell the model to state when evidence is insufficient.
Prompt injection can occur when untrusted retrieved text contains instructions aimed at the model.
Retrieved content should generally be treated as data, not as higher-priority instructions.

SECTION: Reasoning and task decomposition
Complex tasks can be divided into smaller subtasks.
Task decomposition can separate retrieval, extraction, calculation, verification, and final response generation.
Intermediate structured representations can reduce ambiguity between subtasks.
Checklists can remind a model to verify required fields or constraints.
Self-verification prompts can ask a model to check its draft against explicit criteria.
Critique-and-revise workflows generate a draft and then evaluate it against requirements.
Tool-assisted workflows can delegate calculations or database queries to deterministic systems.
Reasoning instructions should focus on useful task behavior rather than requiring unnecessary hidden reasoning.
Verification is especially valuable when the output depends on precise facts or calculations.
Decomposition can increase latency and token usage, so it should be used when it provides measurable value.

SECTION: Prompt evaluation
Prompt evaluation compares outputs produced under different prompt designs.
A fixed test set makes prompt comparisons more consistent.
Evaluation criteria should be defined before comparing prompt variants.
Exact-match accuracy is useful for tasks with deterministic target labels.
Human evaluation can assess quality when multiple outputs are valid.
Groundedness evaluation checks whether factual claims are supported by provided evidence.
Format compliance checks whether required schemas or structures are followed.
Robustness testing varies wording, input order, and irrelevant details.
Adversarial testing can reveal failures caused by ambiguous or malicious inputs.
Prompt changes should be evaluated on representative data rather than a few hand-picked examples.

SECTION: Common prompting techniques
Role prompting gives the model a defined functional perspective such as tutor, analyst, or extractor.
Instruction prompting directly states the desired operation.
Few-shot prompting provides examples of desired behavior.
Chain-of-thought prompting has historically been used to encourage multi-step reasoning, but production systems should not require disclosure of private reasoning.
Self-consistency can compare multiple generated solutions when a task benefits from alternative reasoning paths.
Reflection or critique workflows ask the model to review an initial output.
Prompt chaining sends the output of one stage into another task stage.
Retrieval-augmented prompting supplies external evidence.
Tool calling lets a model invoke deterministic or external capabilities.
Constrained generation limits the output to required labels or structures.

SECTION: Failure modes and safety
Ambiguous instructions can lead to inconsistent outputs.
Conflicting instructions can cause the model to prioritize the wrong requirement.
Prompt injection attempts to alter model behavior through untrusted input.
Data leakage can occur if sensitive context is unnecessarily placed in prompts.
Overly long prompts can exceed context limits or dilute important information.
Prompt brittleness occurs when small wording changes produce large behavior changes.
Example leakage can cause a model to copy an example rather than solve the new task.
Unsupported facts can appear when a prompt asks the model to answer beyond available evidence.
Overly restrictive prompts can reduce useful responses or cause unnecessary refusals.
Prompts should be tested against realistic edge cases and adversarial inputs.

SECTION: Practical prompt patterns
A QA prompt can specify the question, retrieved context, answer format, and grounding rule.
A summarization prompt can specify source text, target length, audience, and factuality requirement.
An extraction prompt can specify entity types, schema, and handling of missing values.
A classification prompt can specify allowed labels and the criteria for each label.
A rewriting prompt can specify the target tone, audience, and information that must remain unchanged.
A comparison prompt can request a neutral attribute-by-attribute table.
A tutoring prompt can request an explanation followed by an example and practice question.
A coding prompt can specify language, input-output requirements, constraints, and tests.
A translation prompt can specify source language, target language, terminology, and formatting.
A document-analysis prompt can specify evidence requirements and source references.
